title: Playing relaxed Dixieland and the importance of tempo
summary: He imitates nobody, likes a relaxed two-beat tempo, and the interviewers ask about favorite tempos and the New Orleans drop.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: No, I just played from my heart, Dick. I still do. When I play I don't try to imitate anybody. I just play the way I feel. And the more relaxed a group is that I'm with, the better I feel about it. I don't like to have to extend myself to keep up with a group. I like to play relaxed music. Well what makes it relaxed? Well you just play what you feel, Dick. When you get to the point where you're extending yourself to reach notes, it's no longer relaxed. And then it gets to be work. You know what I mean, Paul? When you've got to extend yourself to reach them high notes and make, put so much stuff, I tell you I see a lot of good men that play good Dickson and music. They go modern, you know what I mean? And they try to put so much in the damn room until it just confuses their style. They don't sound good anymore. What about tempo? Well that's very essential. The tempo is very essential. If you don't have tempo you don't have anything.
What's the fastest you like to play? Could you just clap it with your hands or beat it with your feet?
Well I don't go very much for fast music unless it's a standard that has to be played fast, like Tiger Rag or some standard that was written fast. But I like a two beat tempo, it's relaxed.
